summary.text: A meteotsunami is a tsunami-like sea wave caused by weather, when rapid changes in air pressure push a body of water out of place.
Severe thunderstorms, squalls and storm fronts set them off, typically when the bad weather moves at the same speed and direction as the waves heading for shore.
They lack the energy of earthquake tsunamis and stay local, but shallow shelves, bays and resonance can enlarge them into hazardous waves.

facts.label: US East Coast
facts.value: About 25 strike each year on average

facts.label: Great Lakes
facts.value: About 126 events a year on average

facts.label: Local names
facts.value: Rissaga in Catalan, abiki in Japanese

items.prompt: A squall line races toward the coast at the same speed and in the same direction as the waves. Why should harbour staff pay attention?

options.label: This is the typical setup for a meteotsunami
The wind will flatten the waves before they land
It only matters if an earthquake strikes too
The next tide will cancel out any big wave

items.explain: Meteotsunamis typically occur when severe weather moves at the same speed and direction as the local waves heading for shore.

items.prompt: In a meteotsunami, what actually pushes the water out of place?

options.label: Heavy rain adding water
A quake beneath the storm
Rapid air pressure changes
Lightning heating the sea

items.explain: They form when rapid changes in barometric pressure displace a body of water.

items.prompt: Records list only a small share of past tsunamis as caused by weather. Why might the real share be higher?

options.label: Weather waves always vanish before reaching land
Many past events have unknown origins or were labelled seiches
Storms were much rarer in earlier centuries
Earthquake records were kept far less carefully

items.explain: Many historical tsunamis have unknown origins, old events are hard to validate, and meteotsunamis may have been misclassified as seiches.

items.prompt: On average, about how many meteotsunami events occur on the Great Lakes each year?

options.label: About 1
About 12
About 126
About 1,260

items.explain: The Great Lakes see about 126 a year on average, even more than the roughly 25 on the US East Coast.

items.prompt: Where is a meteotsunami most likely to grow dangerously large?

options.label: In deep open ocean far from any coast
Along a steep coast with deep water close in
In a small round pond with no inlet at all
In a long, narrow bay lined up with the waves

items.explain: Places whose natural resonance matches the waves, such as long narrow bays facing the oncoming wave, are most susceptible.

items.prompt: Compared with a tsunami from a major earthquake, a meteotsunami usually...

options.label: crosses whole oceans to distant shores
has local effects because it carries less energy
cannot form on lakes, only on seas
is always taller and far more deadly

items.explain: Meteotsunamis lack the energy of significant seismic tsunamis, so their effects are local.
